author: Brian Hioe
title: Taiwanese Continue to Be Detained in China After the End of Their Formal Sentences
content:
TAIWANESE ACADEMIC Tsai Chin-shu has returned to Taiwan, nearly eight years after his arrest in China. Tsai was the head of the Southern Taiwan Union of Cross-strait Relations Associations and director of the Kaohsiung Cross-Strait Exchanges Research Association. Tsai also held a Ph. D from Xiamen University’s Graduate Institute for Taiwan Studies, one of China’s major research centers about Taiwan. Tsai’s return was made known by a post by him on social media earlier this month.

In his capacity as head of these organizations, Tsai was, in fact, apparently an advocate of political unification between Taiwan and China. The Southern Taiwan Union of Cross-strait Relations Associations advocates closer political and economic relations between Taiwan and China and was a supporter of the Ma administration’s efforts at establishing closer ties with China, as observed in the organization’s support of the 2015 Ma-Xi meeting.

Tsai was detained on charges of endangering Chinese state security and was detained by Chinese authorities in July 2018 after crossing into Xiamen, China from Kinmen in order to attend a cross-strait food fair. author: Brian Hioe
title: Does the Trump-Xi Meeting Show the Outcome of Over-Reliance on the US?
content:
THE TRUMP-XI MEETING that took place in Washington DC over the weekend largely proved to be a non-event. Relatively little of consequence was remarked upon by the two leaders, except the two sides committing to reduce tariffs on some 30 billion USD worth of goods.

If Taiwan hoped to keep out of the limelight, one notes that in the course of the meeting, Xi Jinping did seek to convince the US of historical ties between the two countries–even if the “China” that Xi referred to was actually the Republic of China, rather than the People’s Republic of China. Trump himself claimed that the two leaders had not spent much time discussing Taiwan.

What proved more of a curveball, however, was later comments to Fox News by US ambassador to China, David Perdue, who stated that Trump had offered to sell US arms to China in the course of their conversation. Perdue claimed that this was not the first time that Trump had made such comments to Xi before and that this had come up before past meetings. Nevertheless, Perdue also emphasized that US policy on Taiwan remained unchanged. Trump now denies that this ever took place.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does China Intend to Target Taiwan With New National Security Legislation?
content:
TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT officials, speaking under conditions of anonymity to the media, have warned that China may roll out national security legislation directed at Taiwan in the coming months. Such national security legislation would follow up on China’s recently passed ethnic unity law.

The law criminalizes actions aimed at disrupting a vaguely defined “national unity”. Although initial warnings were that the law was mainly aimed at Tibetans and Uyghurs, the Lai administration has framed such national security legislation as potentially a threat to Taiwan. Under such laws, after all, support for Taiwanese independence–or even just maintaining Taiwan’s current democratic freedoms and its de facto independence–could be construed as illegal and criminal under the law.

Such Taiwanese government officials have pointed to a number of laws, some of which are still in the review process, as potentially impacting Taiwan. This includes the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration, Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security, and National Defense Mobilization Law.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Did the KMT Reverse Course on Drone Spending?
content:
AFTER MUCH political contention about the budget earlier this year–including Taiwan’s defense spending–the KMT eventually relented and passed the national budget after over 200 days of stalling at the end of last month. Though the KMT had originally proposed cutting or freezing drone spending–in fact, suggesting that it might cut or freeze all budget that would have been allocated to drones, this did not come to pass.

The KMT seemed to have suddenly become aware of the poor optics of blocking drone spending after an article in The Economist, which lashed out at the KMT as obstructionist and self-interested for continuing to block drone spending when this could be vital to Taiwan’s defense against Chinese threats. In short order, then, the KMT legislative caucus suddenly had a reversal of course.

Nevertheless, the KMT’s approval of drone funding places this under the central government budget, rather than as a special budget. The original special expenditure for drone spending that the Lai administration originally hoped to pass was 210 billion NT for three specific drone systems, which would have been unmanned aerial vehicles and maritime drones.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will There Be Increased Discussion of Climate Resilience in Taiwan?
content:
A RECENT ARTICLE in the New York Times ranked Taipei lowest out of the 72 cities that it assessed in terms of climate preparedness. In the wake of the article, the two Taipei mayoral candidates–Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT–have traded barbs on what it would take to make Taipei more prepared. Chiang largely attempted to play up the accomplishments of his mayoral administration to date, while Shen has called for proactive measures.

Indeed, there has not been much discussion to date of climate preparedness in Taiwan. The particularities of the Taiwanese political context have led much discussion about environmentalism to be confined to discussing Taiwan’s energy mix, with the issue of nuclear energy remaining contentious.

The issue of nuclear waste storage has long been controversial, in that Taiwan has a limited land mass, as a result of which local communities end up being foisted with nuclear waste storage facilities. The impact of the 2011 Tohoku typhoon and tsunami led to increased consideration in Taiwan of what could occur if there were a catastrophic tsunami or earthquake, such as led to the meltdown of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear reactor.

On the other hand, discussion of the suitability or unsuitability of Taiwan for nuclear energy has largely cleaved along partisan lines in past decades. In more recent times, however, the DPP has reversed course

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will Kuai Kuai Workers Strike?
content:
WORKERS AT ONE of Taiwan’s best-known snack companies, Kuai Kuai, have voted in favor of a strike.

The strike authorization takes place after an announcement by the company that it would be selling the land on which its existing factory sits on in Zhongli and moving to Hsinchu. The two sites are 39 kilometers from each other, meaning that the move is untenable for many workers.

In particular, workers were only informed of the land scale on September 1st. According to the Ministry of Labor, the move was not expected for another two years. The factory has operated in Zhongli since 1968, and 1/3rd of workers at Kuai Kuai have worked there for more than thirty years, despite the fact that their wages are near minimum wage.

The land sale is ironic. Namely, the land will be sold to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. At a time when the semiconductor sector is dominant, as fueled by the AI boom, this has led to significant land acquisitions by semiconductor companies.

Yet Kuai Kuai is an iconic snack in the technology industry. Namely, it is a common superstition in Taiwan that bags of Kuai Kuai can prevent machines and equipment from malfunctioning. It is ironic that Kuai Kuai workers are being thrown under the bus by the very industry the snack is associated with.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: Dear Sherry: A Daybreak Digital Memorial
content:
The following letter serves as a digital memorial to Sherry Yue (she/they; 邱梓榳 Chiu Zi Ting, known affectionately as 玥餅 Yuèbǐng by her friends), who died by suicide on April 16, 2026 at the age of 26. It is written by one of Sherry’s friends and fellow trans activists, Yo-Ling Chen, a contributing editor at New Bloom who worked with Sherry and an early iteration of the Trif Trans Bar team to establish Taiwan’s first trans bar in New Bloom’s events/community space, Daybreak (破曉咖啡). Sherry was a minimalist, vegetarian, front-end engineer who enjoyed reverse-engineering things for fun, and someone who loved life with an adventurous passion the year before her departure.

I am so, so sorry that I missed your funeral…

I know that you wouldn’t want to see me beating myself up over this, and I also know that you would have appreciated the various kinds of work I was buried under that led to the insomnia, which led to me mixing up the funeral time, which led to me arriving to an empty ceremony hall at the exact moment your body was in the final stages of cremation. I rushed to the crematorium hoping that I would at least see a part of you one last time—a single wisp of smoke from the chimney, that would have been enough. But that’s not how modern crematoriums work.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will New Changes Improve Taiwan’s Image on Migrant Work?
content:
A NUMBER OF changes are set to occur in the migrant work landscape in Taiwan going forward.

For one, the first batch of migrant workers in the hospitality field has arrived, consisting of 35 Indonesians. These 35 workers arrived in Taiwan as part of the new Multinational Skilled Worker Enhancement Program and are classified as skilled labor, rather than blue-collar migrant workers. The 35 workers previously conducted internships in Taiwan of at least one year in length and are required to reach A-2 level listening and speaking within three years, per the requirements of the program.

Their employer, Regent Taipei, previously hired them as interns, and it approached them individually under the new program. The 35 workers are mostly in their twenties and will return to the departments they worked in. The terms of the new program specify that hospitality industry businesses can hire a new migrant worker if they increase the salary of their lowest-paid Taiwanese worker by 2,000 NT, though hiring of migrant workers is still capped at 10% of the workforce.

The hospitality industry, which has a shortfall of 6,000 workers annually, has long clamored for hiring migrant workers to take up positions that Taiwanese are no longer interested in working. author: Jeremy Ray Jewell
title: A Singapore Contract, Beijing’s Red Lines
content:
APPLY TO TEACH for Polly English and, before entering a classroom, the platform presents a screen titled “Sensitive Content Compliance Agreement.” Under “DO NOT Talk about,” it prohibits discussion of “Political issues, including Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macao, Xizang (Tibet), and Xinjiang.”

The next section is harder to dismiss as ordinary classroom etiquette. Under “Consequences of Violation,” the screen lists “Immediate termination of my Service Agreement,” “Potential legal action,” and “Responsibility for any resulting damages.” It does not say what kind of legal action, which damages might qualify, or how far those consequences reach. A teacher working outside the PRC is asked to accept an open-ended legal and financial warning for discussing some of Beijing’s most sensitive political questions.

Nothing on that screen is presented as PRC law. Polly English describes itself as an online English teaching company based in Singapore, and its teacher terms name Little Moon Pte. Ltd. as the contracting party and place the agreement under Singapore law and Singapore courts. That makes the arrangement more revealing, not less: recognizable PRC political red lines appear inside a private contract governed somewhere else.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will the National Contact Point System Help Resolve Wrongdoing by Taiwanese Companies Abroad?
content:
AT THE START of this month, Taiwanese and Indonesian groups submitted the first complaint to the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) under the new National Contact Point (NCP) complaint system. As the name implies, the system designates the MOEA as the place where complaints about wrongdoings by Taiwanese companies internationally should be directed. Nevertheless, the Taiwanese government was criticized for announcing that the MOEA would serve as Taiwan’s NCP in September 2024, but delaying its actual rollout.

A number of criticisms from Indonesian groups centered around Taiwanese companies in the environmentally destructive nickel mining industry. Among the groups present were Action for Ecology and People Emancipation, the FSPIM Morowali Labour Union, as well as Fagawene, a local organization based out of the Weda Bay Area.

Nickel mining is a highly carbon-intensive endeavor, and it is reliant on coal-burning power plants. In addition to air pollution, wastewater discharge has led to coral deaths. This has damaged fishing grounds, killed coral reefs, and impacted river and lake ecosystems in Sagea. Tourist sites such as the Boki Maruru Cave have also been put at risk of irreversible damage. Deforestation affects residential areas, worsening issues of flooding while depriving local communities of access to clean water.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Taiwan Hits Out at Chinese Checkbook Diplomacy, Even as Also Engaging In It
content:
ACCORDING TO TAIWANESE national security officials, leaked Chinese government documents show the extent to which China engages in checkbook diplomacy.

Specifically, in an interview with the Liberty Times, National Security advisor Alex Huang comments on documents that purport to show Beijing offered Micronesia 1 million yuan–subsidizing the purchase of a vehicle. This was reportedly in exchange for blocking Taiwan’s participation in the World Health Organization.

Other documents in the leaked tranche of documents appear to show China’s influence over African Union countries. The documents apparently show that the African Union accepted 200 million yuan in a “renovation grant” from China, but sought further funding in order to upgrade its headquarters, to the tune of 50 million USD.

Efforts by China to constrain Taiwan’s diplomatic influence in Africa have become increasingly visible, especially after a trip to Eswatini by President Lai Ching-te for the 40th anniversary of King Mswati III’s accession to the throne was canceled at the last minute. This was because the Seychelles, Mauritius, and Madagascar revoked overflight privileges for Lai’s aircraft at the last minute, though Lai later traveled to Eswatini aboard Mswati III’s personal plane at a later date.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Foodpanda Accused of Docking Worker Pay Over Delivery Delays
content:
THE MINISTRY OF LABOR has warned Foodpanda over docking worker pay for delayed deliveries. In particular, Foodpanda delivery drivers currently face pay being docked for delays of between one to five minutes. The Ministry of Labor, however, has stated that after reviewing cases of labor violations, Foodpanda could be fined between 20,000 NT and 100,000 NT.

This is far from the first time that there have been labor disputes over the issue of pay calculation. Gig economy platforms such as Foodpanda and Uber Eats have consistently been accused of using unclear formulas in order to carry this out.

Last month, delivery workers accused Uber Eats of using unlawful payment calculation formulas, citing cases in which workers were only paid for the delivery time of one order, rather than both orders that they were handling at the time. This would violate new regulations that took effect on July 21st, which require not only hourly compensation at a rate of 245 NT per hour, a wage 1.25 times the minimum wage, as well as at least a minimum payment of 45 NT per order. The new laws were hailed by the Taiwan Delivery Industry Union Alliance and the National Delivery Industrial Union as a victory after six-and-a-half years of campaigning when they were passed earlier this year.

Indeed, Foodpanda’s actions also run afoul of the same laws that were passed on July 21st.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will There Be Corruption Cases in 2026 Elections?
content:
A NUMBER OF recent cases touch on questions of corruption ahead of the upcoming local elections. In particular, issues of corruption remain rife at the local level, and it is probable that there will be vote buying in the election–as occurs with any Taiwanese election.

New Taipei City Councilor Yang Chun-mei of the KMT has become the first politician to fall afoul of laws against vote buying, over accusations that she distributed laundry detergent and other household goods to voters. Campaign finance laws specify that the worth of goods distributed by politicians to voters cannot exceed a certain amount, as a result of which such goods usually consist of tissues, paper fans, and other low-value items.

Laundry detergent has, in fact, been among the goods distributed by politicians in the past in the form of laundry pods, memorably leading three to be hospitalized after mistaking the laundry pods for candy after a 2024 campaign rally by KMT presidential candidate Hou You-yi. But it appears that Yang distributed household goods in such quantity or otherwise promised financial reward to constituents in return for their votes so as to fall afoul of the law.

Yang is a four-time KMT city councilor representing Plains Indigenous. Though she has since been released on a 500,000 NTN bail, in addition to her, 21 individuals were questioned by prosecutors before the arrest.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Mandarin Training Center Teachers Criticize Reversal On Labor Negotiations by University Administration
content:
MANDARIN LANGUAGE TEACHERS at National Taiwan Normal University’s (NTNU) Mandarin Training Center (MTC) continue to be in a deadlock with the university administration. Specifically, after the second round of labor negotiations between the university and teachers, the university has reversed course.

Previously, it had appeared that NTNU’s administration was prepared to admit that teachers should be covered by the Labor Standards Act. Now, however, the university does not want to account for past periods in which teachers should have been covered by the Labor Standards Act, but claims that teachers will be covered by it only starting in September.

In particular, the Ministry of Labor informed NTNU that teachers at the MTC should be covered by the Labor Standards Act in November 2024. It took collective action for the administration to take action, however, teachers held a press conference and began to publicly organize in March of this year. MTC students have often been supportive and helped teachers campaign.

NTNU was fined by the Taipei City Department of Labor for violations in July. According to the teachers’ union at MTC, however, the university administration has continued to reject proposals about minimum working hours, employment protections, and teaching materials.
